summary.intent: Deep-research the release-management tool landscape (Changesets, Knope, Nx Release, release-please, others) and compare it against Callisto's actually verified behavior, to assess market fit and readiness for a v1 alpha from a developer/monorepo-owner point of view.
summary.outcome: The session was still in the research phase and no final report had been produced. It gathered competitor info via web search, registry/GitHub API checks and sub-agents, and checked Callisto's docs and source, reaching preliminary findings on positioning, differentiators and limitations.

repo: Callisto is a Rust workspace (crates/callisto-cli, callisto-graph, callisto-model) with docs under docs/ (config.md, stability.md, publishing.md, architecture/release.md, architecture/polyglot-v1.md, projects/ROAD-TO-V1.md).
Documented adoption limits: no Windows support, token-based publishing only, and a gap between commit-inferred version bumps and release PRs.
The managed release-PR path rejects active prerelease mode. This is a user-visible limitation beyond what the README states.
Callisto's most distinctive area is its release-recovery model, plus cross-ecosystem (Cargo, npm, PyPI) dependency updates and publishing that are reviewable and recoverable.

Release-related logic lives in crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release_pr.rs, crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/execute.rs, crates/callisto-graph/src/cascade.rs, crates/callisto-graph/src/groups.rs (linked/fixed groups) and crates/callisto-model/src/release_transition.rs.
Native resolution behavior is covered by crates/callisto-cli/tests/native_resolution.rs.

code.finding: Managed release-PR flow; this is where the rejection of active prerelease mode was verified.
Dependency cascade logic, read to validate how version bumps propagate.
Init behavior, read to evaluate onboarding and adoption effort.
Status command, read to confirm what is a real end-to-end user-facing command.

workflow: The research workflow pairs the repo's own docs and source (to validate claims) with web search and registry/GitHub API queries for current competitor versions and releases.
The Entire local research/brain index was unavailable, so the source was used directly.

Competitor findings changed the picture: Knope already combines changesets with multi-language support, Nx has file-based version plans, Changesets v3 preserves package.json formatting, and pnpm has built-in change files and monorepo versioning. Together these weaken the case for an npm-only repo to switch to Callisto.
Sub-agents (spawn_agent/interact_agent) were used in parallel for research.

friction: Entire's local research index (brain brief) was unavailable, forcing a fallback to reading source directly.
Locating the research-report schema and guide files in the plugin cache took several searches (repeated rg attempts).
Feature claims in the docs had to be checked against the implementation, since some features exist as CLI commands but do not work end to end.
open_items: Produce the final structured research report (the schema is research-report@1.json), covering market fit and where Callisto is ahead and behind.
Finish checking the remaining Callisto claims (cascade, peer escalation, preserve-npm-ranges, linked groups, registry confirmation) against the implementation.
Address the gaps found: Windows support, trusted/OIDC publishing instead of tokens, commit-inferred bumps vs release PRs, and prerelease support in the release-PR path.
Decide on positioning, given that Knope, Nx, Changesets and pnpm already cover much of the npm-only use case.
